query: Platinum-group metals can promote distinct reactions, and earlier PGM-based nanoscale catalysts showed strong activity, selectivity, and durability in complex catalysis. A representative catalyst was reported to perform particularly well in ethanol oxidation, which involves 12-electron and 12-proton transfers, but these performance reports did not establish a comprehensive causal explanation of its behavior during operation. Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs its catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Define an unnamed controlled change with a suitable baseline, the predicted observations, the reaction regime in which the hypothesis should apply or fail, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing lattice strain in high‐performance hollow Pt‐based nanostructures shifts the ethanol oxidation reaction from incomplete to complete (CO2) oxidation by altering the adsorption energies of oxygenated intermediates.
generation.material_initial_state: Pd@PtRh multimetallic nanorings with pronounced hollow morphology and high inherent lattice strain.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal annealing treatment under an inert atmosphere to partially relax lattice strain while maintaining the overall nanoring morphology and particle dispersion.
generation.conditions: Operando electrochemical testing in acidic ethanol electrolyte over potentials covering both water dissociation and ethanol oxidation regimes, with simultaneous in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR).
generation.structural_mediator: Modulation of lattice strain in the Pt-based alloy shell induced by thermal treatment, with minimal change to electrochemically active surface area.
generation.mechanism: Reduced lattice strain weakens the binding of poisoning intermediates (e.g., CO) and optimally tunes Pt–OH adsorption, thereby facilitating water dissociation and enabling more efficient removal of adsorbed CO; this shift in adsorption energetics promotes the 12-electron oxidation pathway leading to higher CO2 selectivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed catalysts exhibiting lower lattice strain will show decreased in situ signals for CO adsorption, lower onset potentials for water dissociation, and an increased yield of CO2 (as observed via real-time product analysis) compared to as-synthesized nanorings with higher strain.
generation.baseline: As-synthesized Pd@PtRh nanorings with high lattice strain operating under identical electrochemical conditions in acidic ethanol electrolyte.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective at potentials where water dissociation is significant and the dynamic formation/desorption of oxygenated intermediates dominates; at very low potentials, where such intermediates are less involved, the strain effect may be negligible.
generation.uncertainty: Combines evidence from studies reporting the enhanced performance of hollow Pt‐based nanostructures (PMC8170318::web::001::introducion) and those linking promotional effects of oxygenated species (PMC6273622::web::021::5_conclusions). The novel aspect is the targeted modulation of lattice strain via post-synthesis annealing to decouple electronic structure effects from surface area; however, it is uncertain if annealing can reliably reduce strain without adversely affecting dispersion or ECSA.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Pd@PtRh nanorings; subject one set to controlled thermal annealing (designed to partially relax lattice strain) while keeping the other as-synthesized. Perform operando XAS to quantify lattice strain, in situ FTIR to monitor the intensity of adsorbed CO and OH species, and DEMS for product analysis during ethanol oxidation in acidic media.
measurements: Quantification of lattice strain via X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and/or in situ XRD under working potentials
FTIR spectral intensity for adsorbed CO and OH species as a function of potential
Onset potential and current density profiles from cyclic voltammetry
Product distribution analysis (CO2 vs. acetaldehyde/acetic acid ratios) via differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally annealed (strain-relaxed) catalysts do not exhibit a decrease in CO-related spectral signals and fail to show an increased formation of CO2 (or if there is a deterioration in electrochemical performance), then the hypothesis that lattice strain modulation governs the shift toward complete ethanol oxidation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The catalytic activity toward the ethanol oxidation reaction (EOR) was found to increase in the following order: Pt/C < Pt–Sn 3:1/C < Pt–Sn 1:1/C. The opposite trend was found for the onset potential of the EOR. In this regard, FTIRS and DEMS analysis showed that the C-C scission occurs at low overpotentials and at the same values independently of the Sn loading. However, the amount of C-C bond breaking decreases with the rise of Sn in the catalyst, which is attributed to the dilution of the active phase. Additionally, both spectroelectrochemical techniques indicate that the catalytic activity and the onset potential for the EOR are improved by the promotional effect of Sn on bimetallic PtSn/C catalysts for the water oxidation reaction. The last provides oxygenated species (OHad) at low overpotentials (about 0.5 V) to liberate the active phase from the main catalyst poison (COad) and to produce acetic acid. Indeed, it was detected that acetic acid and acetaldehyde increases meanwhile carbon dioxide decreases with the Sn loading in the catalyst, indicating that the enhanced catalytic activity toward the EOR is mainly due to the incomplete EOR.

Direct ethanol fuel cells (DEFCs) are an attractive green power source for portable electronic devices since ethanol is a non-toxic liquid with high energy density and easy to be stored and transported (Antolini, ; Brouzgou et al., ). So far, platinum (Pt) have proved to be the most active monometallic catalyst for the ethanol oxidation reaction (EOR). Unfortunately, Pt is highly expensive and extremely scare in earth, severely limiting its extensive use in DEFCs. In addition, Pt is vulnerable to some intermediates and reaction byproducts (e.g., CO) during the EOR process, which will dramatically decrease its catalytic activity (Iwasita and Pastor, ; De Souza et al., ; Farsadrooh et al., ). These limitations push us to design advanced Pt-based catalysts with excellent catalytic properties and optimal utilization efficiency of Pt for EOR. One of the most promising strategies is to boost the intrinsic catalytic ability of noble-metal atoms by optimizing the composition, surface structure, and strain distribution (Kua and Goddard, ; Rossmeisl et al., ).
